prompt: `Raw.java` put a year into a raw `List` of titles. When did anything complain?
hint: Three commands ran.

choices.text: `javac` refused to compile it
choices.why: It compiled, with two `Note:` lines that are easy to read past.

choices.text: Only at run time, with a `ClassCastException` at the cast
choices.why: Right: and the stack trace named line 17, not line 10 where the year went in.

choices.text: Never: the program printed the year as a title
choices.why: It printed two titles and failed on the third element.

prompt: The mistake in `Raw.java` was on line 10 and the exception named line 17. How many lines apart are they?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: With `List<String>` written in, where did `Typed.java` fail?
hint: Before anything ran.

choices.text: At run time, on the first `toUpperCase`
choices.why: It never ran: the compiler stopped it.

choices.text: At compile time, on line 15, where the titles are read
choices.why: The reading line was fine; the error was where the year went in.

choices.text: At compile time, on line 10, at the wrong `add`
choices.why: Right: `int cannot be converted to String`, on the line that was actually wrong.

prompt: A colleague's build prints `Note: Library.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations.` on every run, and they want to ignore it. What does it mean?
hint: What did `-Xlint:unchecked` reveal in `Raw.java`?

choices.text: Some line let an unchecked value into a generic collection
choices.why: Right: recompile with `-Xlint:unchecked` to see which line, as section 02 did.

choices.text: The file is too long for the compiler to check fully
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it; the note is about raw or unchecked uses.

choices.text: The file uses a feature that will be removed in a future JDK
choices.why: That is a deprecation warning, a different message.

prompt: In `public class Box<T>`, what is `T`?
hint: It is chosen by each use of `Box`.

choices.text: A class called `T` that must be imported
choices.why: There is no class `T`; it is a name for a type chosen later.

choices.text: A type parameter, a name for a type chosen later
choices.why: Right: `Box<String>` chooses `String` for it.

choices.text: Shorthand for `Object`, written shorter
choices.why: At run time it becomes `Object`, but in the source it is checked as the type each use chose.

prompt: Why does `max` declare `T extends Comparable<T>` rather than just `T`?
hint: Which method does the loop call on `item`?

choices.text: So that `max` can only be called with strings
choices.why: It was called with `Integer`s too; the bound allows any comparable type.

choices.text: So that `item.compareTo(best)` is allowed to compile
choices.why: Right: without the bound, only `Object`'s methods are callable on a `T`.

choices.text: So that the method runs faster on numbers
choices.why: Bounds change what compiles, not how fast it runs.

choices.text: Because every type parameter must have a bound
choices.why: `Box<T>` has none, and compiled.

prompt: `max(List.of(new Member("Ana"), new Member("Bruno")))` did not compile. What would make it compile, without touching `max`?
hint: The message said what `Member` lacked.

choices.text: Casting the list to the raw type: `max((List) members)`
choices.why: That turns it into a raw type, the unchecked use section 02 warned about.

choices.text: Declaring the list's type with `var`
choices.why: `var` infers the same `List<Member>`; the bound still fails.

choices.text: Making `Member` implement `Comparable<Member>`
choices.why: Right: then `T` can be `Member`, and the bound holds.

prompt: In `Box<String> box = new Box<>();`, the empty `<>` on the right is called the ___.
hint: A shape of a gem.

prompt: You need a method that returns the last element of any list. Which signature is right?
hint: The method needs nothing from the elements.

choices.text: `static <T extends Comparable<T>> T last(List<T> items)`
choices.why: The bound demands something `last` never uses, and refuses lists of `Member`.

choices.text: `static <T> T last(List<T> items)`
choices.why: Right: no bound, because nothing is called on the elements, and the caller gets its own type back.

choices.text: `static Object last(List<Object> items)`
choices.why: A `List<String>` is not a `List<Object>`, and the caller would have to cast the result.

prompt: Why did `total(fines)` fail to compile when `total` took a `List<Number>` and `fines` was a `List<Integer>`?
hint: Generic types and subtypes.

choices.text: Because an `Integer` is not a `Number`
choices.why: It is; the issue is between the lists, not the elements.

choices.text: Generic types are invariant: `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`
choices.why: Right: otherwise `total` could add a `Double` to a list of integers.

choices.text: Because `List.of` returns an unmodifiable list
choices.why: Unmodifiable lists pass type checks like any other; the types themselves did not match.

prompt: Inside `total(List<? extends Number> amounts)`, which line does not compile?
hint: The method does not know which type the list really holds.

choices.text: `Number n = amounts.get(0);`
choices.why: Reading as `Number` is exactly what `? extends Number` allows.

choices.text: `int k = amounts.size();`
choices.why: `size` does not depend on the element type.

choices.text: `amounts.add((Number) 7);`
choices.why: Right: the list might be a `List<Double>`, so nothing can be added to it.

choices.text: `for (Number n : amounts) {}`
choices.why: Iterating reads, and reads are allowed.

prompt: PECS: a parameter the method reads from is a producer and takes `? ___ T`; one it writes into is a consumer and takes `? super T`.
hint: Producer, the first letter of PECS's second word.

prompt: `copy(all, fines)` compiled with `all` a `List<Number>` and `fines` a `List<Integer>`. What was `T`?
hint: `from` is `List<? extends T>`, `to` is `List<? super T>`.

choices.text: `Integer`
choices.why: Right: `fines` produces `Integer`s, and a `List<Number>` is a list of a supertype of `Integer`.

choices.text: `Object`, the only type both lists share
choices.why: The compiler infers the most specific type that fits, and `Integer` fits.

choices.text: `Number`, since `all` is a list of numbers
choices.why: `Number` also fits; the section's text says `T` was inferred as `Integer` and then `Double`.

prompt: Match each parameter's use to the type the section's table gives for it.
hint: Producer extends, consumer super.

prompt: What did `titles.getClass() == years.getClass()` print, for a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>`?
hint: What does the JVM know of the brackets?

choices.text: `false`
choices.why: At run time the type arguments are gone, and both are `ArrayList`.

choices.text: `true`
choices.why: Right: one class, `java.util.ArrayList`, whatever was in the brackets.

choices.text: It did not compile, since `==` cannot compare classes
choices.why: Comparing two `Class` objects with `==` is ordinary, and it printed a value.

prompt: `javap -c Box` showed the field `item` as `Ljava/lang/Object;`. Then how did `String title = box.take();` get a `String` safely?
hint: Look at the instruction after the call.

choices.text: The JVM remembers that this `Box` was created as `Box<String>`
choices.why: It does not: `getClass()` showed no type argument at all.

choices.text: `take()` converts its result to the right type itself
choices.why: `take` returns an `Object`; it knows nothing of `String`.

choices.text: The compiler put a `checkcast String` in `UseBox`, after the call
choices.why: Right: the check moved from the class to each caller, where the type is known.

prompt: Why is `return new T();` a compile error inside `Limits<T>`?
hint: What would the JVM need to know?

choices.text: At run time there is no `T` to say which class to create
choices.why: Right: the type argument was erased, and `new` needs a real class.

choices.text: `T` might be an interface, which cannot be created
choices.why: That is a possible problem, but the error is about any `T` at all: `required: class`.

choices.text: Generic classes are not allowed to create objects
choices.why: `UseBox` created a `Box` without trouble; only `new T()` is refused.

prompt: Which of these does type erasure forbid? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anything that needs `T`, or the type argument, at run time.

choices.text: `o instanceof List<String>` on an `Object o`
choices.why: Yes: the list does not carry its element type, so the check cannot be made.

choices.text: `o instanceof List<?>` on an `Object o`
choices.why: No: it only asks whether `o` is a list, which the JVM knows.

choices.text: Two methods `f(List<String>)` and `f(List<Integer>)` in one class
choices.why: Yes: once erased their signatures are identical.

choices.text: A field of type `List<String>`
choices.why: No: fields of a parameterised type are everywhere in this lesson.

prompt: A method prints every element of any list, and never adds to it. Which parameter type fits best?
hint: It reads only `Object`'s `toString`.

choices.text: `List<Object>`
choices.why: A `List<String>` is not a `List<Object>`, so most callers could not pass theirs.

choices.text: `List<?>`
choices.why: Right: any list is accepted, and its elements are read as `Object`.

choices.text: `List`, the raw type, which accepts anything
choices.why: It accepts anything and turns the checks off; `List<?>` accepts anything and keeps them.

prompt: Put what happens to `String title = box.take();` in order, from source to running program.
hint: Check first, erase after.
items: `javac` writes a `checkcast String` after the call in the caller
The JVM runs `take`, then the cast, at run time
